## Design

### 2026-11-02: My plan for the final project is to build a 4-bit binary adder/subtracter.

**1.5h**

My plan for the final project is to build a 4-bit binary adder/subtracter.
I know from my A Level CS how full adders work, and also the process of binary subtraction with two’s complement, so I’m really excited to be able to put this theory into practice and make a VERY basic computer (well sort of)!

I will use a breadboard and logic gate ICs for this. No cheaping out and just buying adders. No – purely logic gates and a lot of wires for this!

I started today therefore by planning this project and determining feasibility. I really liked the idea of a programmable 4- or 8-bit computer on a breadboard but felt that was too complicated. I could have also chosen something else since it turns out this is now freestyle week (I had wondered about a games controller) but decided against it. This is a nice and different project, which means I've covered PCBs, 3D printing, analogue signal processing, software+hardware combo, displays and breadboard logic!

I then began to sketch out the plan. This will use 4 full adders wired together. Input B will pass through an XOR gate for all of the adders, with the other XOR input coming from K, a control line. When this is high (1), the system will count the second number as one to subtract instead. K will also be passed into the carry in input of the first full adder. This will result in finding the two's complement of the second number (thus making it negative), and then adding the two together to effect subtraction!

### 2026-11-03: Logic Logic Logic!

**1.5h**

Logic Logic Logic!

I have spent a lot of time today working out this adder. I settled on using Mokxi.com to design this, since I can eventually convert it to some kind of breadboard schematic and generate a set of simple instructions that I should be able to follow when I build this for real.

After lots of logic gates and wiring, I have the full adder/subtracter working! It was so cool to run my tests and see it actually work.

![4-bit-adder-subtracter](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EBuChAcUkspX5zhs3qEVPUNL9stbHepB/15dd60182aa6595c08554532ae0014129f7430d29f806b0275f7972aced46c71.png)

The next thing I am going to work on is a memory. I of course need to balance physical complexity, but I should be okay to make this for real. I am going to make a memory function, using master-slave D Flip Flops which I will build by hand with logic gate ICs. This will store the last calculation and, if I can figure it out, allow you to add something to the last stored value in memory.

### 2026-11-04: Okay, prepare yourself - this is going to be complicated.

**2h**

Okay, prepare yourself - this is going to be complicated.

Today I have almost finished laying out the logic and getting the thing working. What follows is a brief explanation of each part - what it is, and how it works.

---

![4-bit-adder-subtracter](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EBuChAcUkspX5zhs3qEVPUNL9stbHepB/15dd60182aa6595c08554532ae0014129f7430d29f806b0275f7972aced46c71.png)

This is the 4-bit adder/subtracter. Each of the four modules is capable of adding two 1-bit numbers, and a carry bit. The first adder sends its carry bit into the carry in of the second adder, and so on. The final adder sends its carry bit to an output LED for overflow.
The input B is XORd with a control signal, K, to allow subtraction. The easiest way to do binary subtraction on this level is using two's complement. This is where you flip each bit of the number to be subtracted, and add one, making it into its two's complement (a signed way to show negative numbers in binary) equivalent. The really clever part is how the add one is implemented. The carry in bit for the first adder takes input from the control line, meaning that a 1 is automatically added to the result (instead of added to the second number - this works because of the associativity of addition). Pretty neat, huh?

---

![register](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EBuChAcUkspX5zhs3qEVPUNL9stbHepB/e9c2368d1605151e9f125a6844e38c99797e6b6a15d2f6a7ea15476cf37d9f8a.png)

The second part of this system is the memory. I have implemented a basic 5-bit accumulator (ACC) to store the result of the previous calculation. This is again done only with logic gates. The ACC is made up of 5 Master-Slave D Flip-Flops, each taking input from the output of the four adders and the fourth carry out bit. Where this gets clever is how values are added to the accumulator.
Usually, such a flip-flop uses a clock signal to change its state. When the clock signal is low, the state is locked, no matter what signal goes into the input. However, when the clock signal is high, the value can be changed to match the input signal. I only want my accumulator to store the value once the calculation is done. The output LEDs light up and change as you enter the numbers to calculate with, hence the need for a master-slave design. Instead of a clock giving the write-allow signal, though, a button provides it. It functions in exactly the same way, but implements the functionality of a STORE button.

---

![just multiplexers](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EBuChAcUkspX5zhs3qEVPUNL9stbHepB/27e360c58a0e2d197407eb026b3fcc2a14df66bce9fb782b3c2ad9113a335a7e.jpg)

The final part of this system that I implemented today is the ability to calculate with the value stored in memory. To do this, we need to be able to take input from either the Input A switches, or from memory, leaving B unchanged (since we can turn B into a negative number to be subtracted. This is how a real calculator behaves). To do this, the circuit uses four 2-to-1 multiplexers. These can be seen above the A and B input switches on the above image. They take input from A, the ACC and the memory-read mode switch. They output the values from the Input A switches **UNLESS** the mode switch is high, in which case, they override the A values with the values from the ACC. This passes these values back into the adder as input A.

---

I ran a series of tests on this, and got halfway through them, but noticed some buggy behaviour. I had initially added a multiplexer for the stored carry bit, but realised we don't want or need that, so removed it. However, something isn't quite working when you try to subtract a number from the value retrieved from memory, so I'm going to need to fix that. But that will have to happen tomorrow!

### 2026-11-05: Breadboardin Time

**2h**

Breadboardin Time

My favourite part of Breadboard was when Breadboard said 'It's Breadboardin' Time' and Breadborded all ove the place...

Sadly today, I have had to scale back a little bit. I just couldn't get the memory-feed-back-into-adder system working properly. It was creating feedback loops and getting messed up and generally just behaving weirdly. I'm already out of my comfort zone a little here, and I could not fix this! But if there's one thing this event has taught me, it's when to stop and simplify. Now is one of those times!

So, I am just not going to keep this feature. Luckily I had taken backups after every major stage, so reverting the changes was as easy as just loading the backup.

I therefore began to plan how this will work on a breadboard. I decided that I want to lay it out digitally first, so I can make all my design mistakes in a low-stakes environment where I can't accidentally fry an IC. Hopefully this will reduce my risk of damaging anything!
I decided to use TinkerCAD Circuit mode to do this, because it's reasonably simple to use but also decently powerful, and can simulate the circuit which is a nice bonus. Because I designed the circuit first in a simple, logical (haha) layout with logic gate symbols, transferring it to a breadboard and ICs shouldn't be too bad. It hasn't been so far -  the main challenge has been learning how a breadboard works.

### 2026-11-06: Can't lie, my brain hurts!

**2h**

Can't lie, my brain hurts!

Today I've been converting the logic schematic into a digital breadboard (as I mentioned previously - to test it and figure out the problems before I use real hardware). And I'm very pleased to say that I have got the adder fully working!

There is a little bit of funny behaviour with the output LED state getting frozen when the SUB switch is switched OFF from an ON position but I will try and fix that. Nothing terrible though.

I did make a silly mistake yesterday by mixing up Inputs A and B (they were the other way around on the logic schem!). So I had wired up B into the second AND gate on second adder where it should be A. So I had the B XORd with K (SUB line) in one input, and then raw B in the other input. Somehow the adder still worked up to 2 bits, hence I didn't catch it yesterday, but when adding the 3rd bit, the 2 and 3 LEDs would light up when bit 2B was entered. So I figured that out and fixed it.

Tomorrow - I will add the memory module. Then I'll have Sunday to clean up, do bug fixes, then list and cost all the components and do the final admin.

### 2026-11-07: The breadboard is almost done!

**1.5h**

The breadboard is almost done!

With all the adders wired up, I moved on to the memory modules.

Looking at costs and complexity, I came to the sad conclusion (after spending a decent amount of time attempting to wire up the memory using only NAND gates and inverters) that I would need to use Flip Flop ICs instead. These are much simpler but most importantly will work out to be cheaper.

With these wired up and the cap over the push button to reset the memory LEDs on startup, the adder/subtracter is almost done! I tested it and it seems to be all working, apart from a bug with the SUB switch that honestly could just be the simulator.

Now all I have to do is final bug fixes and then admin, costing, etc. But I'm gonna need to find about 200 wires for this which could be... spenny...

### 2026-11-08: Today, disaster struck, and a great tragedy befell me...

**1.1h**

Today, disaster struck, and a great tragedy befell me...

TinkerCad, for some reason unknown to me, had not been autosaving my work since... well... I'm not even sure. But very early on in the project. Which meant that when I loaded it back up, pretty much all of my breadboard plan was gone. Thankfully, this was really just to test the theory and make sure that it would 1) work with ICs on a breadboard and 2) make mistakes digitally so I can avoid frying any chips (since I won't be buying any spares, which is admittedly a little risky). There isn't a way to export the files, either, so I didn't even have any backups.

I therefore spent a little time remaking it from the (thankfully detailed) screenshots I had been uploading to the Half Life journals to a point where I was happy with how it worked. It's nowhere near a finished breadboard design, but it is enough to remind me how the adder will be wired. It's annoying that I won't be able to zoom in on the connections and pull things apart to see exactly how I had laid them out, but between this, my images and the logic diagram, I should be fine in 5-ish weeks' time.

I then spent some time doing the dreaded budgeting and component hunting. Always a lengthy process, but I managed to get it done faster than usual. Definitely making progress there! I am hoping that I will be able to use some bonus coins earned for shipping 1 or 2 projects to purchase a breadboard and wire kit from the Half Life shop. Then I'll just need a power supply and some wires, which will probably be best obtained through the kit which I have included in my BOM. If I can't get breadboards through the shop, the kit has enough, and I'll just have to buy some wires out of pocket.
Finding the ICs was a challenge. For some reason, they just wouldn't show up on LCSC, but eventually, I was able to find the right ones. I've gone with TI chips, which could end up being a little more expensive, but I know that they will work really well and do exactly what I (and the simulators) expect them to do.

So that is the final design week complete! It's looking like I'll have some downtime next week and possibly the week after, until my projects get approved and funding comes through (and the parts arrive... yeah that might take a while), but I'm super excited to get building when they do!

The amount of circuit I remade. Really it was just the switch and power connections I wanted a record of, since the adder is laid out much more cleanly in the logic diagram file anyway.
